Content:
The sum of two independent binomial random variables is a binomial random variable, provided that the variables have equal success probabilities.

Content:
More precisely, if [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p)] are independent, then

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2\sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Content:
We'll prove this in a separate lesson. Notice that the probability of success [MATH: p] must be the same for both variables.

Content:
For example, if [MATH: X_1\sim B({\color{red}{4}},0.5)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B({\color{blue}{3}},0.5)] are independent, then

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼B(4 + 3, 0.5); ∼B(7, 0.5).]

Content:
There is some nice intuition behind this rule. Suppose that [MATH: X_1] represents the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is spun [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}] times, and [MATH: X_2] is the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is spun [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}}] times. Therefore, the random variable

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2]

Content:
represents the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is spun [MATH: {\color{red}{4}} + {\color{blue}{3}} = 7] times. In other words, to calculate the distribution of [MATH: Y,] we add the number of trials, but the probability of success on each trial ([MATH: 0.5]) remains fixed.

Content:
Note: It's possible to extend this result to an arbitrary number of random variables.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_k,] are mutually independent binomial random variables such that

Content:
[MATH: X_i\sim B(n_i,p), \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,k.]

Content:
It can be shown that their sum has the binomial distribution

Content:
[MATH: Y=X_1+X_2+\ldots+X_k\sim B(n_1+n_2+\cdots + n_k,p).]

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: X_1\sim B(6,0.65)] and [MATH: X_2 \sim B(4,0.65)] are independent, and [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2,] what is [MATH: P(Y>7)?] Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: X_1\sim B(6,0.65)] and [MATH: X_2 \sim B(4,0.65)] are independent, and [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2,] what is [MATH: P(Y>7)?] Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent random variables, where [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p),] then

[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2\sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Since [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, we have

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼B(6 + 4, 0.65); ∼B(10, 0.65).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: Y\sim B(n,p),] the probability mass function is given by

[MATH: f(y)=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,n.]

In this case, we have [MATH: Y\sim B(10, 0.65),] so [MATH: Y] has the probability mass function [MATH: f(y)=\binom{10}{y}(0.65)^y(0.35)^{10-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,10.]

To find [MATH: P(Y >7),] we need to find [MATH: f(y)] at [MATH: y=8,9,10.] So, we have

[MATH: P(Y > 7)|= P(Y = 8) + P(Y = 9) + P(Y = 10); = f(8) + f(9) + f(10); = ((10)/(8))(0.65)^{8}(0.35)^{2} + ((10)/(9))(0.65)^{9}(0.35)^{1} + ((10)/(10))(0.65)^{10}(0.35)^{0}; ≈ 0.262.]

items.title: Finding a Sum of Binomial Random Variables in Context

sections.normalized_html: There are two blood donation centers in a certain town. On a particular day, [MATH: 12] donors arrived at the first center, and [MATH: 7] donors arrived at the second center. If it is known that [MATH: 24\%] of the town's population has blood type A+, what is the probability that at least [MATH: 4] of the donors have blood type A+?
sections.readable_text: There are two blood donation centers in a certain town. On a particular day, [MATH: 12] donors arrived at the first center, and [MATH: 7] donors arrived at the second center. If it is known that [MATH: 24\%] of the town's population has blood type A+, what is the probability that at least [MATH: 4] of the donors have blood type A+?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] be the number of A+ donors arriving at centers [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] respectively. Therefore, we have two mutually independent binomial random variables:

[MATH: X_1\sim B(12,0.24),\qquad X_2\sim B(7,0.24).]

Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, where [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p),] then

[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2 \sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Hence, [MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼B(12 + 7, 0.24); ∼B(19, 0.24).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: Y\sim B(n,p),] the probability mass function is given by

[MATH: f(y)=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,n.]

In this case, we have [MATH: Y\sim B(19, 0.24),] so [MATH: Y] has the probability mass function

[MATH: f(y)=\binom{19}{y}(0.24)^y(0.76)^{19-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,19.]

We want to find [MATH: P(Y \geq 4).] The easiest way to do this is to use the complement, which is given by

[MATH: P(X \geq 4) = 1-P(X < 4).]

We have

[MATH: P(Y < 4)|= P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2) + P(Y = 3); = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3); = ((19)/(0))(0.24)^{0}(0.76)^{19} + ((19)/(1))(0.24)^{1}(0.76)^{18}; + ((19)/(2))(0.24)^{2}(0.76)^{17} + ((19)/(3))(0.24)^{3}(0.76)^{16}; ≈ 0.2968.]

Finally, [MATH: P(Y ≥ 4)|= 1 − P(Y < 4); = 0.7032.] Therefore, the probability that at least [MATH: 4] of the donors have blood type A+ is [MATH: 0.7032.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The sum of two independent binomial random variables is a binomial random variable, provided that the variables have equal success probabilities.

Content:
More precisely, if [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p)] are independent, then

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2\sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Content:
We'll prove this in a separate lesson. Notice that the probability of success [MATH: p] must be the same for both variables.

Content:
For example, if [MATH: X_1\sim B({\color{red}{4}},0.5)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B({\color{blue}{3}},0.5)] are independent, then

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼B(4 + 3, 0.5); ∼B(7, 0.5).]

Content:
There is some nice intuition behind this rule. Suppose that [MATH: X_1] represents the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is spun [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}] times, and [MATH: X_2] is the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is spun [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}}] times. Therefore, the random variable

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2]

Content:
represents the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is spun [MATH: {\color{red}{4}} + {\color{blue}{3}} = 7] times. In other words, to calculate the distribution of [MATH: Y,] we add the number of trials, but the probability of success on each trial ([MATH: 0.5]) remains fixed.

Content:
Note: It's possible to extend this result to an arbitrary number of random variables.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_k,] are mutually independent binomial random variables such that

Content:
[MATH: X_i\sim B(n_i,p), \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,k.]

Content:
It can be shown that their sum has the binomial distribution

Content:
[MATH: Y=X_1+X_2+\ldots+X_k\sim B(n_1+n_2+\cdots + n_k,p).]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Distribution of a Sum of Binomial Random Variables

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: X_1\sim B(8,0.7)] and [MATH: X_2 \sim B(5,0.7)] are independent, what is the distribution of [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent random variables, where [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p)], then

[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2\sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Since [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, we have

[MATH: Y|= X_{1} + X_{2}; ∼B(8 + 5, 0.7); ∼B(13, 0.7).]

Item 5 — Example: Computing a Probability Using a Sum of Binomial Random Variables

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: X_1\sim B(6,0.65)] and [MATH: X_2 \sim B(4,0.65)] are independent, and [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2,] what is [MATH: P(Y>7)?] Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent random variables, where [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p),] then

[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2\sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Since [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, we have

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼B(6 + 4, 0.65); ∼B(10, 0.65).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: Y\sim B(n,p),] the probability mass function is given by

[MATH: f(y)=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,n.]

In this case, we have [MATH: Y\sim B(10, 0.65),] so [MATH: Y] has the probability mass function
[MATH: f(y)=\binom{10}{y}(0.65)^y(0.35)^{10-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,10.]

To find [MATH: P(Y >7),] we need to find [MATH: f(y)] at [MATH: y=8,9,10.] So, we have

[MATH: P(Y > 7)|= P(Y = 8) + P(Y = 9) + P(Y = 10); = f(8) + f(9) + f(10); = ((10)/(8))(0.65)^{8}(0.35)^{2} + ((10)/(9))(0.65)^{9}(0.35)^{1} + ((10)/(10))(0.65)^{10}(0.35)^{0}; ≈ 0.262.]

Item 8 — Example: Finding a Sum of Binomial Random Variables in Context

Example Prompt:
There are two blood donation centers in a certain town. On a particular day, [MATH: 12] donors arrived at the first center, and [MATH: 7] donors arrived at the second center. If it is known that [MATH: 24\%] of the town's population has blood type A+, what is the probability that at least [MATH: 4] of the donors have blood type A+?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] be the number of A+ donors arriving at centers [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] respectively. Therefore, we have two mutually independent binomial random variables:

[MATH: X_1\sim B(12,0.24),\qquad X_2\sim B(7,0.24).]

Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, where [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p),] then

[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2 \sim B(n_1+n_2, p).]

Hence,
[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼B(12 + 7, 0.24); ∼B(19, 0.24).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: Y\sim B(n,p),] the probability mass function is given by

[MATH: f(y)=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,n.]

In this case, we have [MATH: Y\sim B(19, 0.24),] so [MATH: Y] has the probability mass function

[MATH: f(y)=\binom{19}{y}(0.24)^y(0.76)^{19-y}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots,19.]

We want to find [MATH: P(Y \geq 4).] The easiest way to do this is to use the complement, which is given by

[MATH: P(X \geq 4) = 1-P(X < 4).]

We have

[MATH: P(Y < 4)|= P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2) + P(Y = 3); = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3); = ((19)/(0))(0.24)^{0}(0.76)^{19} + ((19)/(1))(0.24)^{1}(0.76)^{18}; + ((19)/(2))(0.24)^{2}(0.76)^{17} + ((19)/(3))(0.24)^{3}(0.76)^{16}; ≈ 0.2968.]

Finally,
[MATH: P(Y ≥ 4)|= 1 − P(Y < 4); = 0.7032.]
Therefore, the probability that at least [MATH: 4] of the donors have blood type A+ is [MATH: 0.7032.]
